description: Run a Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter: survey prospects on four price points, plot the curves, and find the optimal price range at the intersection of too-cheap and too-expensive lines.

steps.description: Design the Van Westendorp survey with the four standard questions and a clear product description.

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: Clear description of the product or service being priced

inputs.name: target-audience
inputs.desc: Who will be surveyed (must be actual potential buyers, not random people)

outputs.name: survey-instrument
outputs.desc: The four-question survey with product description, ready to distribute

outputs.name: sample-plan
outputs.desc: How many responses needed (minimum 30, ideally 100+) and how to reach the target audience

process: Write a clear, neutral product description. The respondent must understand what they are pricing. No selling language, no superlatives.

Use the four standard Van Westendorp questions: (1) At what price would this be so cheap you would question its quality? (2) At what price is this a bargain - a great deal? (3) At what price is this getting expensive but you would still consider it? (4) At what price is this too expensive to consider?
Plan to survey actual potential buyers, not friends or colleagues. The responses must represent real purchase intent. Minimum 30 responses for a rough estimate, 100+ for reliable curves.
Include a screening question to verify the respondent is in the target audience. Responses from non-buyers distort the curves.

steps.description: Collect the survey responses and clean the data by removing invalid or inconsistent responses.

inputs.name: sample-plan
inputs.desc: How many responses and from whom

outputs.name: clean-responses
outputs.desc: Valid responses with all four price points per respondent

outputs.name: response-count
outputs.desc: Number of valid responses after cleaning

process: Distribute the survey through the planned channels. Allow 1-2 weeks for collection.

Remove responses where the price points are logically inconsistent: 'too cheap' must be less than 'bargain,' which must be less than 'expensive,' which must be less than 'too expensive.' Inconsistent responses indicate the respondent did not understand the questions.
Remove responses from people who failed the screening question or who completed the survey in under 30 seconds (indicating they did not read the product description).
Record the final count of valid responses. If below 30, the results are directional only, not statistically reliable.

steps.description: Plot the four cumulative distribution curves and find the key intersection points that define the optimal price range.

outputs.name: price-curves
outputs.desc: Four cumulative distribution curves plotted on the same chart

outputs.name: intersection-points
outputs.desc: The four key intersections: Point of Marginal Cheapness, Point of Marginal Expensiveness, Optimal Price Point, and Indifference Price Point

process: For each of the four questions, create a cumulative distribution: at each price point, what percentage of respondents gave that answer or lower?
Plot all four curves on one chart with price on the x-axis and cumulative percentage on the y-axis.

Find the intersections: the Optimal Price Point is where 'too cheap' and 'too expensive' cross. The Indifference Price Point is where 'bargain' and 'expensive' cross. The range between Marginal Cheapness and Marginal Expensiveness is the acceptable price range.
The Optimal Price Point is not necessarily the price you should charge. It is the price at which resistance from both directions is minimized.

steps.description: Interpret the price range and decide where within it to set the actual price, based on positioning strategy.

outputs.name: recommended-price
outputs.desc: The recommended price with the rationale for where it sits within the acceptable range

outputs.name: pricing-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this specific price was chosen (premium positioning, market penetration, competitor alignment, etc.)

process: The acceptable range (Marginal Cheapness to Marginal Expensiveness) is where you should price. Below this range, prospects question quality. Above it, they refuse to consider.

Where within the range depends on strategy: price at the high end for premium positioning (fewer customers, higher margins), at the low end for market penetration (more customers, lower margins), or at the Optimal Price Point for minimum resistance.

Compare the range to competitor pricing. If competitors are priced below your acceptable range, your product has perceived value differentiation. If they are within the range, you need other differentiation.
Set the price and document the rationale. The Van Westendorp data gives you empirical backing for the price, which is useful for internal debates and investor conversations.

steps.description: Re-run the Van Westendorp analysis periodically to detect shifts in price sensitivity as the market evolves.

outputs.name: monitoring-schedule
outputs.desc: When to re-run the analysis (annually, or after a major market change)

outputs.name: drift-indicators
outputs.desc: Signs that price sensitivity has shifted: conversion rate changes, competitor price movements, customer feedback patterns

process: Schedule a re-run annually or after a major market change (new competitor, economic shift, product update).

Between re-runs, monitor drift indicators: if conversion rate drops without other changes, the price may have crossed the acceptable range. If customers stop mentioning price in objections, you may be underpriced.
When re-running, survey a new sample. Do not re-survey the same people; their anchoring to the previous price distorts the results.
Compare the new curves to the previous ones. If the acceptable range has shifted upward, you have room to raise prices. If downward, you may need to adjust or add value.

description: Calculate revenue per constraint hour: identify the bottleneck resource, calculate revenue per hour of that resource for every product or client, and prioritize the highest-revenue-per-constraint-hour work.

steps.description: Identify the one resource you cannot add more of that limits your total output.

inputs.name: business-description
inputs.desc: What your business or practice does and how it generates revenue

inputs.name: resource-inventory
inputs.desc: All resources used in delivering your product or service (people, equipment, time, capital)

outputs.name: constraint-resource
outputs.desc: The single resource that limits total output (the one you would add more of first if you could)

outputs.name: constraint-capacity
outputs.desc: How many hours of the constraint resource are available per week

process: List all resources used in delivery. For a solopreneur, the constraint is almost always your own time. For a service firm, it might be senior partner hours. For a manufacturer, it might be a specific machine.
The constraint resource is the one where: if you had more of it, you would produce more revenue, and you cannot easily add more. It is the bottleneck.
Measure the available capacity: how many hours per week does this resource operate? For a person, it is working hours minus meetings, admin, and other non-revenue time.
This number is your denominator. Every product, service, and client will be measured against it.

steps.description: Calculate the revenue per constraint hour for every product, service, or client.

outputs.name: revenue-per-hour-table
outputs.desc: Every product, service, or client ranked by revenue generated per hour of the constraint resource consumed

outputs.name: total-revenue-capacity
outputs.desc: Maximum possible weekly revenue if all constraint hours were allocated to the highest-revenue work

process: For each product, service, or client, calculate: total revenue divided by total constraint hours consumed. A $10,000 project that takes 20 hours of constraint time generates $500/constraint-hour. A $5,000 project that takes 5 hours generates $1,000/constraint-hour.
Rank from highest to lowest revenue per constraint hour.
Calculate theoretical maximum: if all available constraint hours were allocated to the highest-ranked item, what would total revenue be? This is your ceiling.
The gap between your theoretical maximum and your actual revenue is the cost of misallocation. You are spending constraint time on lower-value work when higher-value work exists.

steps.description: Reallocate constraint hours from low-revenue-per-hour work to high-revenue-per-hour work.

inputs.name: revenue-per-hour-table
inputs.desc: Products/clients ranked by revenue per constraint hour

outputs.name: reallocation-plan
outputs.desc: Which work to take more of, which to reduce, which to stop, and which to delegate to non-constraint resources

outputs.name: expected-revenue-increase
outputs.desc: The projected revenue increase from reallocation

process: Identify work in the bottom quartile of revenue per constraint hour. For each item, ask: can this be delegated to a non-constraint resource? Can the price be raised? Can it be discontinued?
Identify work in the top quartile. For each item, ask: can we get more of this type of work? What limits the volume? Is the constraint the only bottleneck or are there other limits?
Move constraint hours from bottom-quartile work to top-quartile work. Even a 10% shift can produce significant revenue increases because the per-hour value difference is large.
For work that cannot be stopped but has low constraint-hour revenue, find ways to reduce the constraint hours it consumes: standardize, templatize, or redesign the workflow.

steps.description: Use the revenue-per-constraint-hour data to adjust pricing: underprice high-demand/low-constraint work, overprice work that consumes disproportionate constraint time.

outputs.name: price-adjustments
outputs.desc: Specific price changes for products or services that are mispriced relative to their constraint consumption

outputs.name: adjusted-revenue-per-hour
outputs.desc: The updated revenue per constraint hour after price changes

process: Items with high demand and high revenue per constraint hour may be underpriced. Test a 10-20% price increase and measure volume impact.

Items with low revenue per constraint hour and high constraint consumption are overconsuming the bottleneck. Raise the price until either: the revenue per constraint hour is acceptable, or the client leaves (freeing constraint time for better work).
Do not feel guilty about raising prices on constraint-heavy work. The alternative is that the constraint spends its time on lower-value activity, which hurts the whole business.
Recalculate the full table after price changes to verify the reallocation improved the average revenue per constraint hour.

steps.description: Set up ongoing tracking so you continuously monitor revenue per constraint hour and catch misallocation early.

outputs.name: tracking-system
outputs.desc: How to track constraint hours per product/client on an ongoing basis (weekly or monthly)

outputs.name: rebalance-triggers
outputs.desc: Thresholds that trigger a reallocation review (e.g., any new client consuming more than 20% of constraint hours at below-average revenue per hour)

process: Set up weekly time tracking for the constraint resource, categorized by product or client. This takes 5 minutes per day but provides the data for continuous optimization.
Calculate revenue per constraint hour monthly. Plot it over time. A declining trend means new work is lower-value, or existing work is consuming more constraint time.
Define triggers: if any single product or client drops below 50% of the average revenue per constraint hour, flag it for review.
Review the full table quarterly. The market changes, clients evolve, and new opportunities appear. The ranking should be re-evaluated regularly.

description: Price based on value delivered to the customer, not cost incurred by you. Quantify the economic value your product creates for the customer, then price at a fraction of that value.

steps.description: Understand the customer's economics: how they make money, what their costs are, and where your product fits in their value chain.

inputs.name: customer-profile
inputs.desc: Who the customer is and what their business or life looks like

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: What your product or service does for them

outputs.name: customer-economics
outputs.desc: How the customer generates revenue, their cost structure, and where your product saves them money or helps them earn more

outputs.name: value-mechanism
outputs.desc: The specific mechanism by which your product creates value (saves time, reduces errors, increases revenue, reduces risk, improves quality)

process: Interview 5-10 customers (or prospective customers) about their economics. Ask: how do you make money? What are your biggest costs? What would happen if [the problem your product solves] got 50% worse? What would happen if it got 50% better?

Identify the specific value mechanism. Your product does one or more of: saves time (which has a dollar value), reduces errors (which have a cost), increases revenue (which is measurable), reduces risk (which has an expected cost), or improves quality (which affects pricing or retention).

Quantify the value mechanism in the customer's terms, not yours. 'Our software saves 10 hours per week' means nothing. 'Our software saves 10 hours per week of a $75/hour employee, which is $39,000 per year' means something.

Verify the quantification with the customer. Ask: 'Does $39,000 per year in savings sound about right based on your experience?' If they say it is higher, you have more pricing room. If lower, adjust.

steps.description: Quantify the total economic value your product delivers per year per customer.

outputs.name: annual-value-per-customer
outputs.desc: The dollar amount of value your product creates per customer per year (the value ceiling)

outputs.name: value-confidence
outputs.desc: How confident you are in this number (based on how many customers confirmed it)

process: Calculate the annual value using the formula: [quantity of value unit saved/gained per week] x [dollar value per unit] x 52 weeks.
Include all value mechanisms, not just the primary one. If your product saves time AND reduces errors AND improves quality, sum all three.
Discount for risk: if the value depends on the customer using the product correctly (which not all will), reduce the number by the expected adoption rate.
The result is the value ceiling: the maximum the customer should be willing to pay if they captured 100% of the value. Your price will be a fraction of this.

steps.description: Set the price as a fraction of the value delivered, choosing the fraction based on competitive alternatives and customer power.

outputs.name: price-as-value-share
outputs.desc: The price stated as a percentage of value delivered (typical range: 10-30% of value)

outputs.name: pricing-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this specific share was chosen (competitive landscape, customer alternatives, switching costs)

process: The standard value-share range is 10-30% of the value delivered. At 10%, the customer keeps 90% of the value and has a strong incentive to buy. At 30%, the deal is less obvious but still favorable for the customer.

Choose the percentage based on: competitive alternatives (if competitors offer similar value, you need to share more with the customer), switching costs (if switching to you is easy, charge less; if hard, you can charge more), and the customer's sophistication (sophisticated buyers will calculate the value themselves).

State the price in terms of value: 'This costs $12,000 per year and saves you approximately $50,000 per year. You keep 76% of the value.' This framing makes the price feel like an investment, not a cost.
If the value share exceeds 30%, reconsider. At that point, the customer's ROI may not be compelling enough to overcome inertia and risk.

steps.description: Create the materials that communicate the value case to the customer: the ROI calculation, the value comparison, and the proof points.

outputs.name: roi-calculator
outputs.desc: A simple calculator the customer can use to estimate their specific value (input their numbers, see their ROI)

outputs.name: value-proof-points
outputs.desc: 3-5 customer examples showing the actual value delivered (with permission)

process: Build a simple ROI calculator: the customer inputs their specific numbers (team size, hourly rate, error rate, etc.) and sees the estimated annual value and payback period. This makes the value tangible and specific to their situation.
Collect value proof points from existing customers: 'Customer X saved $47,000 in the first year.' Real numbers from real customers are more convincing than your own estimates.
Create a one-page value summary that shows: the problem, the cost of the problem, how your product solves it, the expected value, the price, and the net value retained by the customer.
Train anyone involved in selling to lead with the value conversation, not the feature list. Features describe what the product does. Value describes what the customer gets.

steps.description: Track whether customers are actually realizing the promised value after purchase, and adjust pricing or product if not.

outputs.name: realization-rate
outputs.desc: What percentage of the promised value customers actually capture (ideally 80%+)

outputs.name: value-gap-actions
outputs.desc: If realization is below 80%, specific changes to improve it (better onboarding, feature improvements, customer success intervention)

process: At 90 days and 12 months after purchase, check in with customers: are they seeing the expected savings, revenue increase, or risk reduction?
Calculate the realization rate: actual value captured divided by predicted value. If it is below 80%, there is a gap between promise and delivery.

If the gap is caused by low adoption (the customer is not using the product fully), invest in onboarding and customer success. If the gap is caused by overestimation (the value model was too optimistic), adjust the model downward and reprice.
High realization rates justify price increases. If customers consistently capture 120% of the expected value, you are underpriced.

description: Test price elasticity empirically: raise the price by 10%, measure the volume change, calculate elasticity. Most businesses are underpriced because they fear a volume loss that does not actually happen.

steps.description: Measure the current price, volume, and revenue as the baseline before any test.

inputs.name: product-to-test
inputs.desc: The product or service whose price you want to test

outputs.name: baseline-metrics
outputs.desc: Current price, units sold per period, total revenue per period, conversion rate (if applicable)

outputs.name: baseline-period
outputs.desc: The time period measured and whether it is representative (not a seasonal peak or trough)

process: Record the current price, units sold per month (or per quarter), total revenue, and conversion rate for at least 3 months of data.
Verify the period is representative. Do not baseline during a holiday season, a promotion, or an unusual period. You need the normal run rate.
If you have a subscription product, measure both new signups and churn separately. Price changes affect them differently.
Record the customer acquisition cost if known. A price increase that reduces volume but increases profit per customer may still be the right move.

steps.description: Design the price test: increase by 10%, measure for a defined period, and determine the sample size needed for a reliable result.

outputs.name: test-design
outputs.desc: The test parameters: new price (10% higher), test duration (minimum 30 days), how volume will be measured, and what constitutes a conclusive result

outputs.name: decision-criteria
outputs.desc: The specific thresholds: if volume drops by less than X%, the price increase is net-positive for revenue

process: Set the test price at 10% above current. This is large enough to measure an effect but small enough that it will not cause a dramatic reaction.

Define the test duration: minimum 30 days for products with short purchase cycles, 60-90 days for longer cycles. The test must be long enough for the price change to be noticed by the full buying population.
Define the decision criterion: a 10% price increase is revenue-positive as long as volume drops by less than 10%. Calculate the exact break-even volume drop for your margins.
If possible, run an A/B test (show the new price to half the audience). If not possible, run a before-after test with the full audience.

steps.description: Run the price test and monitor volume daily to detect any sharp drops early.

outputs.name: test-results
outputs.desc: Volume, revenue, and conversion rate during the test period at the new price

outputs.name: volume-change-percentage
outputs.desc: The actual percentage change in volume compared to baseline

process: Implement the price change and start tracking volume daily.
If volume drops more than 20% in the first week, the price increase may be too aggressive for this product. Consider reducing to a 5% increase.
Monitor customer feedback during the test. A few complaints are normal. A surge of complaints or cancellations is a signal to stop the test.
At the end of the test period, calculate the volume change, revenue change, and profit change compared to baseline.

steps.description: Calculate the price elasticity of demand and determine whether the price increase should be kept.

inputs.name: test-results
inputs.desc: Volume and revenue during the test

outputs.name: elasticity-coefficient
outputs.desc: The price elasticity: percentage change in volume divided by percentage change in price. Below 1.0 means inelastic (price increase is profitable). Above 1.0 means elastic (price increase lost revenue).

outputs.name: keep-or-revert-decision
outputs.desc: Whether to keep the new price, revert, or test a smaller increase

process: Calculate elasticity: (% change in volume) / (% change in price). If you raised the price 10% and volume dropped 5%, elasticity is 0.5 (inelastic - keep the increase).
Inelastic (below 1.0): the price increase is profitable because the revenue gain from higher price exceeds the revenue loss from lower volume. Keep the new price.
Elastic (above 1.0): the price increase lost revenue because the volume drop was too large. Revert to the old price or test a smaller increase.
If inelastic, consider testing another 10% increase. Many businesses are significantly underpriced and can sustain multiple increases before hitting the elastic threshold.

steps.description: Monitor elasticity over time because it changes with market conditions, competition, and product evolution.

outputs.name: monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: How to detect shifts in elasticity without running formal tests (churn rate changes, conversion rate trends, competitive price movements)

outputs.name: retest-schedule
outputs.desc: When to re-run the elasticity test (annually, or when market conditions change significantly)

process: Set up ongoing monitoring of the proxy signals: conversion rate trend, churn rate trend, and price-related support tickets or objections.

If conversion rate starts declining without other changes, elasticity may be increasing (customers becoming more price-sensitive). This could be caused by new competitors, economic changes, or declining perceived value.
Schedule a formal re-test annually or after significant market changes.
Over time, build a historical record of elasticity measurements. This gives you a model of how your customers respond to pricing, which informs all future pricing decisions.

description: Analyze where your next dollar of spending should go by comparing the marginal return of each spending category. The next dollar goes to the category with the highest marginal return, not the highest total return.

steps.description: List every spending category and the current allocation to each.

inputs.name: budget-data
inputs.desc: Current spending by category (marketing, R&D, operations, sales, admin, personal categories, etc.)

inputs.name: time-period
inputs.desc: The period being analyzed (monthly or quarterly)

outputs.name: spending-table
outputs.desc: Each category with its current spending and the primary return metric (revenue generated, time saved, risk reduced)

outputs.name: total-spend
outputs.desc: Total spending across all categories

process: List every spending category. Include both obvious categories (marketing, sales) and hidden ones (time spent on admin, opportunity cost of activities).
For each category, record the current spending per period.
For each category, identify the primary return metric. Marketing returns revenue. Training returns skill. Insurance returns risk reduction. Choose one metric per category.

If you are doing this for personal finances, the categories might be: housing, food, transportation, education, health, entertainment, savings. The return metric for each is the value it adds to your life per dollar spent.

steps.description: For each category, estimate the return of the NEXT dollar spent, not the average return of all dollars spent.

inputs.name: spending-table
inputs.desc: Categories with current spending and return metrics

outputs.name: marginal-returns
outputs.desc: For each category: the estimated return of the next $100 (or next $1000) spent, based on diminishing returns analysis

outputs.name: diminishing-returns-notes
outputs.desc: For each category: at what spending level do returns start to diminish significantly

process: The marginal return is NOT the average return. If marketing has spent $10,000 and generated $50,000 in revenue (5x average return), the NEXT $1,000 might only generate $2,000 (2x marginal return) because the easy opportunities have been captured.

Estimate the marginal return by looking at the most recent spending increment. What was the return on the last $1,000 added to this category? This is a better estimate of the next $1,000 than the overall average.
For categories where you have never varied the spending, estimate by asking: if I doubled this spending, would the return double? If not, marginal returns are diminishing.

Note the diminishing returns curve for each category. Most categories follow an S-curve: low returns at first (learning/setup), high returns in the middle (sweet spot), diminishing returns at the top (saturation).

steps.description: Move spending from categories with low marginal returns to categories with high marginal returns.

inputs.name: diminishing-returns-notes
inputs.desc: Where each category sits on the diminishing returns curve

outputs.name: reallocation-plan
outputs.desc: How much to move from which categories to which other categories, with the expected net gain

outputs.name: minimum-thresholds
outputs.desc: Minimum spending levels below which a category cannot function (you cannot cut marketing to zero)

process: Rank categories by marginal return, highest to lowest.
Identify categories where you are past the diminishing returns threshold (marginal return is low relative to other categories). These are overfunded.
Identify categories where you are still in the sweet spot (marginal return is high). These are underfunded.

Move dollars from overfunded to underfunded categories. Each dollar moved increases total return because it leaves a low-marginal-return category and enters a high-marginal-return one. Stop when marginal returns equalize across categories.

steps.description: Re-run the marginal analysis periodically because marginal returns shift as spending levels change.

outputs.name: updated-marginal-returns
outputs.desc: New marginal return estimates after the reallocation has been in effect for one period

outputs.name: next-reallocation
outputs.desc: Whether further reallocation is needed or the current allocation is near-optimal

process: After one period with the new allocation, re-estimate marginal returns. The categories you added funding to now have more spending, so their marginal returns may have decreased. The categories you cut from may now have higher marginal returns.
The goal is equilibrium: all categories have roughly equal marginal returns. At equilibrium, there is no reallocation that would improve total returns.
Perfect equilibrium is not achievable, but each reallocation cycle should move closer to it.
Run this analysis quarterly. The marginal returns shift as market conditions, product offerings, and life circumstances change.

description: Audit customer concentration risk: if any customer represents more than 15% of revenue, you have a concentration problem. Map revenue distribution, identify the risk, and build a diversification plan.

steps.description: Map revenue by customer and calculate each customer's share of total revenue.

inputs.name: revenue-data
inputs.desc: Revenue by customer for the past 12 months

outputs.name: concentration-table
outputs.desc: Each customer's revenue and percentage of total, sorted by share descending

outputs.name: concentration-metrics
outputs.desc: Key metrics: largest customer share, top 3 customer share, number of customers representing 50% of revenue

process: Calculate each customer's total revenue over the past 12 months. Use actual invoiced revenue, not contracted value.
Sort by revenue share descending and calculate cumulative percentage.
Flag any customer above 15% as a concentration risk. Flag the 'whale' (largest customer) specifically.
Calculate how many customers represent 50% of revenue. If the answer is 3 or fewer, concentration is high.

steps.description: For each concentrated customer, model the impact of their departure on revenue, cash flow, and operations.

outputs.name: departure-scenarios
outputs.desc: For each concentrated customer: the revenue loss, the fixed costs that cannot be reduced to match, the cash flow gap, and the time to recover

outputs.name: survival-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether the business could survive the departure of its largest customer without emergency measures

process: For each customer above 15%, model: if they left tomorrow, what is the immediate revenue impact? Which fixed costs cannot be reduced quickly (leases, salaries, committed contracts)?
Calculate the cash flow gap: lost revenue minus reducible costs. This is the monthly burn you would face until replacement revenue is found.
Estimate time to replace: how long would it take to replace this revenue? If the customer is 30% of revenue, replacement might take 12-18 months.
Assess survival: do you have enough cash reserves to cover the gap for the replacement period? If not, the concentration risk is existential.

steps.description: Build a diversification strategy that reduces concentration over 6-12 months without alienating existing large customers.

outputs.name: diversification-plan
outputs.desc: Specific actions to reduce concentration: acquire more small/medium customers, develop new revenue streams, reduce dependency on the largest customer

outputs.name: target-concentration
outputs.desc: The target distribution after 12 months (no customer above 15%, top 3 below 40%)

process: The goal is not to lose the large customer. The goal is to grow the rest of the business so that no single customer represents a dangerous share.
Identify the customer profile of your next 10 ideal customers (similar to your best non-concentrated customers). Focus acquisition efforts on this profile.
Develop at least one revenue stream that does not depend on any single customer: a product, a service tier, or a market segment that distributes across many buyers.
Set 12-month targets: no customer above 15%, top 3 customers below 40% of total revenue. Track monthly.

steps.description: While diversifying, deepen the relationship with large customers to reduce the chance of their departure.

outputs.name: retention-actions
outputs.desc: Specific actions to make each large customer more embedded: multi-contact relationships, expanded use cases, integration depth

outputs.name: early-warning-system
outputs.desc: Signals that a large customer might be at risk of leaving (usage decline, champion departure, competitor engagement)

process: For each concentrated customer, ensure you have relationships with at least 3 contacts (not just one champion). A single-contact relationship is fragile; that person leaving can end the contract.
Expand use cases: if the customer uses you for one thing, help them use you for two or three things. Each additional use case increases switching costs.
Set up early warning monitoring: track usage patterns, contact frequency, and satisfaction signals. A 20% drop in usage over 60 days is an early warning.
Diversification and retention are complementary, not contradictory. You want to keep large customers AND reduce their share by growing everything else.

description: Track expense velocity (the rate of change of spending) rather than just expense levels. A $500/month expense growing at 10% per month is a bigger problem than a $1000/month expense that is flat.

steps.description: Build a time series of each expense category over the past 6-12 months.

inputs.name: expense-data
inputs.desc: Monthly expense data by category for the past 6-12 months

inputs.name: expense-categories
inputs.desc: The categories to track (may be personal or business)

outputs.name: expense-time-series
outputs.desc: Each category's monthly spending plotted over time

outputs.name: category-totals
outputs.desc: Total spending per category over the full period

process: Collect monthly spending data for each category. Use actual transaction data (bank statements, accounting software), not budgeted amounts.
Plot each category as a line over time. Even a simple spreadsheet chart reveals patterns that raw numbers hide.
Include all categories, even ones you think are stable. Creeping expenses often hide in categories you do not monitor because you assume they are fixed.
If data is not available for 6 months, start tracking now and wait. You cannot calculate velocity without at least 3 months of data.

steps.description: Calculate the velocity (monthly growth rate) of each expense category.

outputs.name: velocity-table
outputs.desc: Each category's average monthly growth rate (velocity) and its current monthly level

outputs.name: acceleration-flags
outputs.desc: Categories where velocity is increasing (the growth is accelerating, not just steady)

process: For each category, calculate the average monthly growth rate: (most recent month / earliest month) ^ (1 / number of months) - 1.
A positive velocity means the expense is growing. A negative velocity means it is shrinking. Zero means it is flat.
Flag any category with velocity above 5% per month. At 5% per month, an expense doubles in about 14 months.

Check for acceleration: is the velocity itself increasing? Compare the growth rate of the first half of the period to the second half. Accelerating expenses are more dangerous than steady-growth ones.

steps.description: Project each high-velocity expense 6 and 12 months forward to see where it will be if unchecked.

outputs.name: projections
outputs.desc: For each high-velocity category: what the expense will be in 6 and 12 months at the current growth rate

outputs.name: budget-breach-dates
outputs.desc: When each high-velocity expense will breach its budget or comfort threshold at the current rate

process: For each flagged category, calculate: current monthly amount x (1 + monthly growth rate) ^ 6 for the 6-month projection, and ^ 12 for the 12-month projection.
Compare the projections against budget limits or comfort thresholds. If a $500/month expense at 10% velocity hits $885 in 6 months and $1,569 in 12 months, is that acceptable?
Calculate the budget breach date: the month at which the projected expense exceeds the budget or threshold for that category.
The projections often produce alarming numbers because humans are bad at intuiting exponential growth. A 'small' 8% monthly increase doubles the expense in 9 months.

steps.description: For each high-velocity category, design an intervention that reduces the velocity, not just the level.

outputs.name: interventions
outputs.desc: For each high-velocity category: a specific action that addresses the CAUSE of the growth, not just the current level

outputs.name: target-velocity
outputs.desc: The target growth rate for each category after intervention (ideally 0% or negative)

process: Identify WHY the expense is growing. Common causes: usage creep (more people using a tool), price increases from the vendor, scope creep (doing more without realizing), or lifestyle inflation (spending more because you earn more).
Address the cause, not the symptom. Cutting the expense this month does not help if the velocity remains high. Next month it grows right back.
Set a target velocity for each category. Some categories should be flat (0% growth). Some should shrink (negative velocity). Very few should be allowed to grow unchecked.
Implement the intervention and continue tracking velocity monthly. If the velocity does not decrease within 2 months, the intervention was insufficient.

steps.description: Maintain an ongoing velocity dashboard that flags categories before they become problems.

outputs.name: dashboard-design
outputs.desc: A monthly dashboard showing: each category's current spend, velocity, and 6-month projection, with red/yellow/green flags

outputs.name: review-cadence
outputs.desc: When to review the dashboard (monthly) and what triggers a deeper investigation

process: Build a simple monthly dashboard. For each category, show: current month spend, 3-month average velocity, and 6-month projected spend.
Color-code: green (velocity is 0% or negative), yellow (velocity is 1-5% per month), red (velocity is above 5% per month).
Review monthly. Focus only on yellow and red categories. Green categories are under control.
The dashboard takes 15 minutes per month to update and review. This small investment prevents expense surprises that take much more time and money to fix after the fact.
